To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) maximal muscular power output during burst flight scales negatively with body size, 2) this scaling relationship is less than the scaling relationship for wingbeat frequency, and 3) the scaling relationship for muscular power output is partially offset by a positive scaling of total muscle strain.

the scaling of maximal muscle mass-specific power output during burst flight in Corvidae (M–0,18m) was slightly less negative than the scaling of the wingbeat frequency (–0.29), which is the most commonly cited hypothesis explaining the scaling of avian flight performance, and that muscle strain increased with size (M0.1m), but muscle stress did not (M0.02m).
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanical basis of the scaling of avian locomotor performance.
the evolution of avian flight and how it relates to body size.
the scaling of mechanical power output in birds, and the underlying mechanisms that determine the scaling of flight performance in birds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the scaling relationship of muscular mechanical power is not fully understood and warrants further investigation.

size does not appear to be an absolute constraint on flight performance, but rather that size has significant implications for flight performance that are mediated by a combination of morphological, physiological, and biomechanical factors.
wingbeat frequency is a significant factor in determining maximal power output, but it is not the only factor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the power output of avian pectoralis muscle scales less negatively with body size than the scaling of the wingbeat frequency.
muscle function changes to compensate for the detrimental effects of size.
the scaling relationship of power output is more complex than previously thought, and may not be fully explained by a single mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scaling patterns of mechanical power output in the avian pectoralis muscle are not simply a function of wingbeat frequency and that muscle function may change with body size to maintain power output.

the power-limiting mechanism is unlikely to be a general explanation for the scaling of avian burst locomotion, and that additional factors, such as the scaling of muscle mass and wingbeat frequency, must be considered.
scaling of mechanical power output is not a universal phenomenon and is likely to be highly dependent on the locomotor task and the muscle group under consideration.
